imc-2012-01.title: A bijection
imc-2012-01.body:
Order sums decreasingly, so that a way of writing $n$ is a partition $(a_1\ge a_2\ge\dots\ge a_k)$ with $a_1+\dots+a_k=n$. Let $P_n$ be the set of partitions of $n$ (so $|P_n|=p(n)$; $P_0$ contains only the empty partition) and let $Q_n\subseteq P_n$ be the set of partitions of $n$ that contain at least one part equal to $1$.

The partitions of $n$ all of whose parts are greater than $1$ are exactly the elements of $P_n\setminus Q_n$, so we must show $|P_n\setminus Q_n|=p(n)-p(n-1)$, i.e. $|Q_n|=p(n-1)$.

Define $\varphi:P_{n-1}\to Q_n$ by appending a part $1$:
$$\varphi(a_1,\dots,a_k)=(a_1,\dots,a_k,1).$$
This is a partition of $n$ (still non-increasing, since all $a_i\ge1$) containing a $1$, so $\varphi$ maps into $Q_n$. (For $n=1$: the empty partition of $0$ goes to $(1)$.)

- $\varphi$ is injective: $(a_1,\dots,a_k,1)$ determines $(a_1,\dots,a_k)$.
- $\varphi$ is surjective: a partition in $Q_n$ has smallest part $1$, i.e. it ends with a $1$; removing that last part gives a partition of $n-1$ which $\varphi$ maps back to it.

Hence $|Q_n|=|P_{n-1}|=p(n-1)$, and the number of partitions of $n$ without a part $1$ is $|P_n|-|Q_n|=p(n)-p(n-1)$. ∎

imc-2012-01.title: Generating functions
imc-2012-01.body:
Let $q(n)$ be the number of partitions of $n$ with all parts at least $2$ ($q(0)=1$). Since $q(n)\le p(n)\le 2^{n}$ (a partition of $n$ is determined by a composition, and there are $2^{n-1}$ compositions), the power series below converge for $|x|<\tfrac12$, and a convergent power series determines its coefficients.

Choosing how many times each part $k$ is used gives Euler's product formulas
$$F(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}p(n)x^n=\prod_{k\ge1}\left(1+x^k+x^{2k}+\cdots\right)=\prod_{k\ge1}\frac1{1-x^k},$$
$$G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}q(n)x^n=\prod_{k\ge2}\frac1{1-x^k}.$$
Therefore $G(x)=(1-x)F(x)$. Comparing the coefficients of $x^n$ ($n\ge1$):
$$q(n)=p(n)-p(n-1).$$ ∎

imc-2012-02.title: Three independent rows and a rank-3 example
imc-2012-02.body:
**Small cases.** For $n=1$ the only matrix is $(0)$, of rank $0$. For $n=2$ the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\ b&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,b>0$; its determinant is $-ab\ne0$, so the rank is $2$.

**Lower bound for $n\ge3$.** Let $M=(m_{ij})$ be such a matrix and let $r_1,r_2,r_3$ be its first three rows. Suppose $c_1r_1+c_2r_2+c_3r_3=0$. Looking at columns $1,2,3$ (where $m_{11}=m_{22}=m_{33}=0$):
$$c_2m_{21}+c_3m_{31}=0,\qquad c_1m_{12}+c_3m_{32}=0,\qquad c_1m_{13}+c_2m_{23}=0,$$
with all the $m_{ij}$ appearing here positive. The first equation shows that $c_2$ and $c_3$ are either both zero or nonzero with opposite signs; similarly for the pairs $(c_1,c_3)$ and $(c_1,c_2)$. If some $c_i\neq 0$, these relations force all three to be nonzero and pairwise of opposite signs, which is impossible for three real numbers. Hence $c_1=c_2=c_3=0$: the three rows are linearly independent and $\operatorname{rank}M\ge3$.

**A matrix of rank $3$.** Take $M=\big((i-j)^2\big)_{i,j=1}^n$. Its diagonal is zero and its off-diagonal entries are positive. Writing $u=(1^2,2^2,\dots,n^2)^T$, $v=(1,2,\dots,n)^T$ and $\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)^T$, the identity $(i-j)^2=i^2-2ij+j^2$ says
$$M=u\,\mathbf 1^T-2\,v\,v^T+\mathbf 1\,u^T,$$
a sum of three matrices of rank at most $1$. So $\operatorname{rank}M\le3$, and by the lower bound it equals $3$.

**Answer:** the minimum rank is $0$ if $n=1$, $2$ if $n=2$, and $3$ if $n\ge3$. ∎

imc-2012-03.title: Parity of the final subgroup
imc-2012-03.body:
Call a move *safe* if after it the selected elements still generate a proper subgroup of $S_n$; a player who makes an unsafe move loses immediately. The game is finite (all $n!$ elements together generate $S_n$), so it ends with somebody's unsafe move.

**$n=2$.** $A$ selects the identity. $B$ must select the transposition, which generates $S_2$; $B$ loses.

**$n=3$.** $A$ selects a $3$-cycle $\sigma$. The subgroup generated is $A_3=\{\mathrm{id},\sigma,\sigma^2\}$. Any transposition together with $A_3$ generates $S_3$ (as $A_3$ has index $2$), so $B$ must pick $\mathrm{id}$ or $\sigma^2$ to survive; $A$ then picks the other one, which is safe since everything selected lies in $A_3$. Now all of $A_3$ is selected and $B$ must select a transposition and loses. So $A$ wins.

**$n\ge4$: $B$ wins.**

*Key observation.* Suppose at some moment the selected elements generate a proper subgroup $H$ and the player to move has no safe move. Then every element of $H$ has already been selected: an unselected $h\in H$ would be a safe move (the generated subgroup would stay $H$). Also no element outside $H$ was selected. So exactly $|H|$ moves have been made.

*B's first move.* Let $g$ be $A$'s first element; $\langle g\rangle$ is cyclic, hence proper ($S_n$ is not cyclic for $n\ge3$).
- If the order of $g$ is even, then $g\ne\mathrm{id}$ and $B$ selects $\mathrm{id}$. The generated subgroup is $\langle g\rangle$: proper, of even order.
- If the order of $g$ is odd, all cycles of $g$ have odd length, so $g$ is an even permutation. $B$ selects $h=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ (possible as $n\ge4$; $h\ne g$ because $h$ has order $2$). Both lie in the alternating group $A_n$, so $\langle g,h\rangle\subseteq A_n$ is proper, and it contains the element $h$ of order $2$, so its order is even.

Call the subgroup obtained after move $2$ $H_2$; it is proper with $|H_2|$ even.

*Afterwards*, $B$ always makes a safe move. He can: when it is $B$'s turn, an odd number $m\ge3$ of moves has been made, and the current subgroup $H\supseteq H_2$ is proper (the game is not over). If $B$ had no safe move, the key observation would give $m=|H|$, but $|H|$ is divisible by $|H_2|$, hence even — a contradiction.

So $B$ never makes an unsafe move; since the game must end, $A$ makes the last move and loses.

**Answer:** $A$ has a winning strategy for $n=2,3$; $B$ has a winning strategy for $n\ge4$. ∎

imc-2012-04.title: Three lemmas
imc-2012-04.body:
Throughout, $f$ is $C^1$ and $f'(t)>f(f(t))$ for all $t$.

**Lemma 1.** It is not true that $f(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$.

*Proof.* Suppose $f(t)\to+\infty$. Choose $T_1$ with $f(t)>2$ for $t>T_1$, and $T_2$ with $f(t)>T_1$ for $t>T_2$. Then for $t>T_2$ we get $f(f(t))>2$, so $f'(t)>2$. Hence $f$ is strictly increasing on $(T_2,\infty)$ and $f(t)-t$ has derivative $>1$ there, so $f(t)-t\to\infty$: there is $T_3>\max(T_2,1)$ with $f(t)>t$ for all $t\ge T_3$.

For $t\ge T_3$ we have $f(t)>t>T_2$, and $f$ is increasing on $(T_2,\infty)$, so $f(f(t))>f(t)$; thus $f'(t)>f(t)>0$, i.e. $(\ln f)'>1$, giving $f(t)\ge f(T_3)e^{t-T_3}>T_3e^{t-T_3}$ for $t\ge T_3$. Applying this at the point $f(t)\ge T_3$:
$$f'(t)>f(f(t))>T_3e^{f(t)-T_3},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad f'(t)e^{-f(t)}>c:=T_3e^{-T_3}>0 .$$
Integrating over $[T_3,t]$: $e^{-f(T_3)}-e^{-f(t)}>c(t-T_3)$. The left side is less than $e^{-f(T_3)}$, while the right side tends to infinity — a contradiction. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** $f(t)<t$ for all $t>0$.

*Proof.* If $f(t)\ge t$ for all $t>0$ then $f\to+\infty$, contradicting Lemma 1; so $f(t_2)<t_2$ for some $t_2>0$. If the lemma fails, $f(t_1)\ge t_1$ for some $t_1>0$, and by the intermediate value theorem applied to $f(t)-t$ there is $t_0>0$ with $f(t_0)=t_0$.

*Case I: $f(t)<t_0$ for some $t\ge t_0$.* Let $T=\inf\{t\ge t_0: f(t)<t_0\}$. Then $f\ge t_0$ on $[t_0,T)$ and there are points $\ge T$ arbitrarily close to $T$ with $f<t_0$, so by continuity $f(T)=t_0$ (also if $T=t_0$). Now $f'(T)>f(f(T))=f(t_0)=t_0>0$, so $f>f(T)=t_0$ on some interval $(T,T+\delta)$. Together with $f\ge t_0$ on $[t_0,T]$, this contradicts the definition of $T$.

*Case II: $f(t)\ge t_0$ for all $t\ge t_0$.* Then for $t\ge t_0$ also $f(f(t))\ge t_0$, so $f'(t)>t_0>0$ and $f(t)\ge f(t_0)+t_0(t-t_0)\to\infty$, contradicting Lemma 1. $\square$

By continuity, Lemma 2 also gives $f(0)\le 0$.

**Lemma 3.** (a) If $f(s_1)>0$ and $f(s_2)\ge s_1$, then $f(s)>s_1$ for all $s>s_2$.
(b) In particular, if $s_1\le 0$ and $f(s_1)>0$, then $f(s)>s_1$ for all $s>s_1$.

*Proof.* (a) Suppose the set $\{s>s_2: f(s)\le s_1\}$ is nonempty and let $S$ be its infimum. Then $f>s_1$ on $(s_2,S)$ and there are points $s\ge S$, arbitrarily close to $S$, with $f(s)\le s_1$. If $S>s_2$ this gives $f(S)=s_1$; if $S=s_2$ then $f(S)\ge s_1$ by hypothesis and $f(S)\le s_1$ by continuity, so again $f(S)=s_1$. Now $f'(S)>f(f(S))=f(s_1)>0$.
- If $S>s_2$: $f'(S)>0$ gives $f(s)<f(S)=s_1$ for $s<S$ close to $S$, and such $s$ lie in $(s_2,S)$, where $f>s_1$. Contradiction.
- If $S=s_2$: $f'(S)>0$ gives $f>s_1$ on some $(S,S+\delta)$, contradicting the choice of $S$ as the infimum.

(b) Take $s_2=s_1$: $f(s_2)=f(s_1)>0\ge s_1$. $\square$

**Main proof.** Suppose $f(f(f(t_0)))>0$ for some $t_0>0$; put $t_1=f(t_0)$, $t_2=f(t_1)$, $t_3=f(t_2)>0$.

*Step 1: if $t_1\le 0$ then $t_2\le0$.* If $t_1=0$, then $t_2=f(0)\le0$. If $t_1<0$ and $t_2=f(t_1)>0$, Lemma 3(b) with $s_1=t_1$ gives $f(s)>t_1$ for all $s>t_1$, in particular $f(t_0)>t_1$, i.e. $t_1>t_1$ — impossible.

*Step 2: $t_2>0$.* If $t_2=0$ then $t_3=f(0)\le0$, false. If $t_2<0$: since $f(t_2)=t_3>0$, Lemma 3(b) with $s_1=t_2$ gives $f(s)>t_2$ for every $s>t_2$. Since $t_0>0>t_2$ we get $t_1=f(t_0)>t_2$, and then $t_2=f(t_1)>t_2$ — impossible.

*Step 3.* By Steps 1 and 2, $t_1>0$ and $t_2>0$. Lemma 2 applied to $t_0,t_1,t_2$ gives $0<t_3<t_2<t_1<t_0$.

*Step 4.* Lemma 3(a) with $s_1=t_1$, $s_2=t_0$ ($f(t_1)=t_2>0$, $f(t_0)=t_1\ge t_1$) gives $f(s)>t_1$ for all $s>t_0$. Lemma 3(a) with $s_1=t_2$, $s_2=t_1$ ($f(t_2)=t_3>0$, $f(t_1)=t_2\ge t_2$) gives $f(s)>t_2$ for all $s>t_1$. Hence for $t>t_0$: $f(t)>t_1$, so $f(f(t))>t_2$, and $f'(t)>t_2>0$. Then $f(t)\ge f(t_0)+t_2(t-t_0)\to+\infty$, contradicting Lemma 1.

Therefore $f(f(f(t)))\le0$ for every $t>0$, and by continuity of $f\circ f\circ f$ also for $t=0$. ∎

imc-2012-05.title: Symmetric factorization and Fermat's equation
imc-2012-05.body:
**Fact 1.** For $m\ge0$, $T_m(Z)=Z^{2^m}+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.
*Proof.* $T_m(Z+1)=(Z+1)^{2^m}+1=Z^{2^m}+\sum_{0<j<2^m}\binom{2^m}{j}Z^j+2$. Every $\binom{2^m}{j}$ with $0<j<2^m$ is even, and the constant term is $2$, not divisible by $4$; by Eisenstein's criterion at $2$, $T_m(Z+1)$ — hence $T_m$ — is irreducible. $\square$

**Fact 2 (Fermat).** There are no positive integers $u,v,w$ with $u^4+v^4=w^2$.
*Proof.* Take a solution with $w$ minimal. If a prime $p$ divides $u$ and $v$, then $p^4\mid w^2$, so $p^2\mid w$, and $(u/p,v/p,w/p^2)$ is a smaller solution; hence $\gcd(u,v)=1$. Then $(u^2,v^2,w)$ is a primitive Pythagorean triple; say $u$ odd, $v$ even. So there are coprime $d>e\ge1$ of opposite parity with
$$u^2=d^2-e^2,\qquad v^2=2de,\qquad w=d^2+e^2 .$$
From $u^2+e^2=d^2$ with $u$ odd: if $d$ were even, $e$ would be odd and $u^2+e^2\equiv2\pmod 4$, while $d^2\equiv0$. So $d$ is odd and $e$ even. Since $\gcd(d,2e)=1$ and $d\cdot 2e=v^2$, both $d$ and $2e$ are squares: $d=f^2$, $e=2g^2$. Next $(u,e,d)$ is a primitive Pythagorean triple with $e$ even, so $e=2hi$, $d=h^2+i^2$ with coprime $h>i\ge1$. Then $g^2=hi$ with $\gcd(h,i)=1$, so $h=k^2$, $i=l^2$, and
$$k^4+l^4=h^2+i^2=d=f^2 .$$
This is a solution with $f\le f^2=d<d^2+e^2=w$, contradicting minimality. $\square$

**The case $a=0$.** The polynomial is $X^{2^{n+1}}+1=T_{n+1}(X)$, irreducible by Fact 1.

**The case $a\ne0$.** Substitute $X=Y-\frac a2$ (this does not affect irreducibility):
$$Q(Y)=\Big(Y-\frac a2\Big)^{2^n}\Big(Y+\frac a2\Big)^{2^n}+1=T_n\big(Y^2-\gamma\big),\qquad \gamma=\frac{a^2}{4}.$$
$Q$ is monic of degree $2^{n+1}$ and even: $Q(-Y)=Q(Y)$.

*Claim: no factor of $Q$ of degree less than $2^{n+1}$ is an even polynomial.* Let $g(Y)=\tilde g(Y^2)$ be a nonconstant even divisor, $Q=g\cdot h$. Then $Q(Y)=g(-Y)h(-Y)=g(Y)h(-Y)$, so by uniqueness of the quotient $h(-Y)=h(Y)$, i.e. $h(Y)=\tilde h(Y^2)$. Thus $T_n(W-\gamma)=\tilde g(W)\tilde h(W)$ in $\mathbb Q[W]$. Since $T_n(W-\gamma)$ is irreducible (Fact 1), $\tilde h$ is constant and $\deg g=2^{n+1}$.

*Also:* $Q$ has no odd factor $g$ (with $g(-Y)=-g(Y)$), because then $g(0)=0$ while $Q(0)=\gamma^{2^n}+1>0$.

Now suppose $Q$ is reducible, and write $Q=\prod_{i=1}^r f_i^{m_i}$ with distinct monic irreducible $f_i$, each of degree $<2^{n+1}$. For a monic $f$ put $f^*(Y)=(-1)^{\deg f}f(-Y)$, again monic, and irreducible if $f$ is. From $Q(-Y)=Q(Y)$ and unique factorization, $f\mapsto f^*$ permutes the $f_i$, preserving multiplicities. If $f_i^*=f_i$, then $f_i$ would be even or odd, which we excluded. So the $f_i$ split into pairs $\{f,f^*\}$ with equal multiplicities. Let $f$ be the product of $f_i^{m_i}$ over one member of each pair. Then $Q=f\cdot f^*$, $\deg f=2^n$ (even, as $n\ge1$), so
$$Q(Y)=f(Y)\,f(-Y).$$
Put $Y=0$: with $b=f(0)\in\mathbb Q$,
$$\Big(\frac a2\Big)^{2^{n+1}}+1=b^2 .$$
Let $c=(a/2)^{2^{n-1}}$, a nonzero rational; then $c^4+1=b^2$. We may take $c,b>0$; write $c=u/v$ in lowest terms with $u,v\ge1$. Then $u^4+v^4=(bv^2)^2$; here $bv^2$ is a positive rational whose square is an integer, hence an integer. This contradicts Fact 2.

Therefore $Q$, and hence $X^{2^n}(X+a)^{2^n}+1$, is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$. ∎

imc-2012-06.title: Homer moves last — and can pair up the moves
imc-2012-06.body:
There are $2012$ coefficients and Albert starts, so Homer makes the last move.

**(a)** $f$ is divisible by $x-2012$ iff $f(2012)=0$, i.e.
$$2012^{2012}+a_{2011}2012^{2011}+\dots+a_1\cdot2012+a_0=0 .$$
When only one coefficient $a_k$ is left (on Homer's last move), this is a linear equation $2012^k a_k=(\text{known number})$ with nonzero coefficient $2012^k$, so Homer can solve it. Homer wins (his earlier moves are arbitrary).

**(b)** Split $f$ into even and odd parts: $f(x)=g(x^2)+x\,h(x^2)$ with
$$g(y)=a_0+a_2y+\dots+a_{2010}y^{1005}+y^{1006},\qquad h(y)=a_1+a_3y+\dots+a_{2011}y^{1005}.$$
Then $f(i)=g(-1)+i\,h(-1)$ with $g(-1),h(-1)$ real, so $f(i)=0$ iff $g(-1)=h(-1)=0$. A real polynomial with root $i$ also has root $-i$ and is divisible by $(x-i)(x+i)=x^2+1$; conversely $x^2+1\mid f$ gives $f(i)=0$. So Homer needs $g(-1)=0$ and $h(-1)=0$.

$g$ has $1006$ free coefficients ($a_0,a_2,\dots,a_{2010}$) and $h$ has $1006$ ($a_1,\dots,a_{2011}$) — both even. Homer's strategy: always answer in the same polynomial Albert just played in. After Albert's move that polynomial has an odd number of free coefficients left, so Homer can do this, and both counts are even again after Homer's move. Hence Homer fixes the last coefficient of $g$ and the last coefficient of $h$. When fixing the last coefficient $a_j$ of $g$, the condition $g(-1)=0$ is linear in $a_j$ with coefficient $\pm1$, so he can satisfy it; the same for $h$. Homer wins.

**Answer: Homer has a winning strategy in both (a) and (b).** ∎

imc-2012-07.title: Telescoping
imc-2012-07.body:
By induction all $a_n>0$. The recursion $a_{k+1}\big(1+(k+1)a_k\big)=k a_k^2$, divided by $a_k$, reads
$$k a_k=\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}+(k+1)a_{k+1}\qquad(k\ge1).$$
Hence $\dfrac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}=k a_k-(k+1)a_{k+1}$ for $k\ge 1$, and the sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}=\frac{a_1}{a_0}+\sum_{k=1}^n\big(k a_k-(k+1)a_{k+1}\big)=\frac12+a_1-(n+1)a_{n+1}=1-(n+1)a_{n+1}.$$

It remains to show $n a_n\to0$. We prove $a_n\le 2^{-n}$ for $n\ge1$ by induction. It holds for $n=1$. If $a_n\le2^{-n}$, then $(n-1)a_n\le (n-1)2^{-n}\le1$, which rearranges to $2n a_n\le 1+(n+1)a_n$, i.e. $\frac{n a_n}{1+(n+1)a_n}\le\frac12$. Therefore
$$a_{n+1}=a_n\cdot\frac{n a_n}{1+(n+1)a_n}\le\frac{a_n}{2}\le 2^{-(n+1)}.$$
So $0<(n+1)a_{n+1}\le (n+1)2^{-(n+1)}\to0$, and the partial sums tend to $1$: the series converges and
$$\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}=1 .$$
**Answer: 1**

imc-2012-07.title: Convergence first, then the limit
imc-2012-07.body:
From the telescoping identity $S_n=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}=1-(n+1)a_{n+1}$ we get $S_n<1$. The terms are positive, so the series converges (bounded increasing partial sums), and in particular its terms tend to $0$: there is $n_0$ with $a_{k+1}/a_k<\frac12$ for $k\ge n_0$. Then $a_n\le C\,2^{-n}$ for a constant $C$ and all $n$, so $(n+1)a_{n+1}\le C(n+1)2^{-(n+1)}\to0$, and $S_n\to1$.

**Answer: 1**

imc-2012-08.title: Coprimality and the multinomial bound
imc-2012-08.body:
Suppose $n!+1\mid(2012n)!$.

The multinomial coefficient $\dfrac{(2012n)!}{(n!)^{2012}}$ (the number of words with $n$ copies of each of $2012$ letters) is an integer, so $(n!)^{2012}\mid(2012n)!$. Since $\gcd(n!+1,n!)=1$, $n!+1$ is coprime to $(n!)^{2012}$, and therefore their product divides $(2012n)!$:
$$(n!+1)\,(n!)^{2012}\ \Big|\ (2012n)!\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n!<n!+1\le\frac{(2012n)!}{(n!)^{2012}} .$$
The multinomial coefficient is one term of the expansion of $(1+1+\dots+1)^{2012n}$ ($2012$ ones), so it is at most $2012^{2012n}$. With $K=2012^{2012}$ this gives $n!<K^n$.

On the other hand $e^n=\sum_j n^j/j!>n^n/n!$, i.e. $n!>(n/e)^n$. So $(n/e)^n<K^n$, i.e. $n<eK$.

Only finitely many $n$ qualify. **Answer: finite.**

imc-2012-08.title: Prime factors of $n!+1$
imc-2012-08.body:
Let $n>2012$ with $n!+1\mid(2012n)!$. Every prime factor $p$ of $n!+1$ satisfies $p>n$ (it does not divide $n!$) and $p\le2012n$ (it divides $(2012n)!$). For such $p$, $p^2>n^2>2012n$, so the exponent of $p$ in $(2012n)!$ is $\lfloor 2012n/p\rfloor<2012$, i.e. at most $2011$. Hence
$$n!<n!+1\le\prod_{n<p\le2012n}p^{2011}\le\Big(\prod_{p\le 2012n}p\Big)^{2011}<\big(4^{2012n}\big)^{2011},$$
using the classical estimate $\prod_{p\le x}p<4^x$. A factorial cannot stay below a geometric sequence $C^n$ for all large $n$ (as $n!>(n/e)^n$), so only finitely many $n$ work. **Answer: finite.**

imc-2012-09.title: The Möbius map $x\mapsto 1-a/x$ as a matrix
imc-2012-09.body:
Write $x_{n+1}=x_1$; the system is $x_j(1-x_{j+1})=a$ for $j=1,\dots,n$.

**$a\le\frac14$ works.** The equation $x(1-x)=a$ has a real root since its discriminant is $1-4a\ge0$; take $x_1=\dots=x_n=x$.

**From now on $a>\frac14$.** Then $a\ne0$, so all $x_j\ne0$ and $x_{j+1}=1-\dfrac a{x_j}$. Let
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}1&-a\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad w_j=\begin{pmatrix}x_j\\1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $Mw_j=\begin{pmatrix}x_j-a\\x_j\end{pmatrix}=x_j\begin{pmatrix}1-a/x_j\\1\end{pmatrix}=x_jw_{j+1}$.

The characteristic polynomial of $M$ is $\lambda^2-\lambda+a$, with non-real roots $\lambda,\bar\lambda=\frac{1\pm i\sqrt{4a-1}}2=\sqrt a\,e^{\pm i\theta}$, where $\theta\in(0,\frac\pi2)$ is given by $\cos\theta=\frac1{2\sqrt a}$, i.e. $a=\dfrac1{4\cos^2\theta}$. Let $e,\bar e$ be corresponding (complex conjugate) eigenvectors; they form a basis of $\mathbb C^2$.

**Necessity.** If a solution exists, then $M^nw_1=(x_1x_2\cdots x_n)\,w_{n+1}=\mu w_1$ with $\mu=x_1\cdots x_n$ real. Write $w_1=\alpha e+\beta\bar e$. The real nonzero vector $w_1$ is not a multiple of $e$ (otherwise $Mw_1=\lambda w_1$ would be non-real), nor of $\bar e$; so $\alpha,\beta\ne0$. From $M^nw_1=\alpha\lambda^ne+\beta\bar\lambda^n\bar e=\mu(\alpha e+\beta\bar e)$ we get $\lambda^n=\bar\lambda^n=\mu$, so $e^{2in\theta}=1$, i.e. $\theta=\frac{k\pi}n$ for an integer $k$. Since $0<\theta<\frac\pi2$, $1\le k<\frac n2$, and $a=\dfrac1{4\cos^2(k\pi/n)}$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $a=\frac1{4\cos^2(k\pi/n)}$ with $1\le k<\frac n2$, so $\theta=\frac{k\pi}n$ and $\lambda^n=a^{n/2}e^{ik\pi}=\bar\lambda^n$ is real. As $M$ has two distinct eigenvalues it is diagonalizable, and $M^n$ has the single eigenvalue $\lambda^n$ on a basis of eigenvectors, so $M^n=\lambda^nI$.

For a real parameter $t$ let $\binom{u_j}{v_j}=M^{j-1}\binom t1$ ($j\ge1$). The entries $u_j,v_j$ are polynomials of degree $\le1$ in $t$, and neither is identically zero (that would make a row of the invertible matrix $M^{j-1}$ zero). So we can choose $t$ such that $u_j\ne0$ and $v_j\ne0$ for $j=1,\dots,n$ (we avoid at most $2n$ values). Put $x_j=u_j/v_j$. The second row of $M$ gives $v_{j+1}=u_j$, hence
$$x_{j+1}=\frac{u_j-av_j}{u_j}=1-\frac a{x_j},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad x_j(1-x_{j+1})=a,$$
and $\binom{u_{n+1}}{v_{n+1}}=M^n\binom t1=\lambda^n\binom t1$ gives $x_{n+1}=t=x_1$. So the cyclic system has a solution.

**Answer:** $a\le\frac14$, or $a=\dfrac1{4\cos^2(k\pi/n)}$ for some integer $k$ with $1\le k<\frac n2$. (For $n=2$ the second set is empty; e.g. for $n=3$ it is $\{1\}$.) ∎

imc-2012-10.title: Petridis' minimal-ratio argument
imc-2012-10.body:
Write $kA=A+\dots+A$ ($k$ times). Since $A$ is finite and nonempty (if $A=\emptyset$ everything is $0$), we can choose a nonempty $B\subseteq A$ for which
$$K=\frac{|A+B|}{|B|}$$
is as small as possible. Taking $B=A$ shows $K\le c$. By minimality, $|A+X|\ge K|X|$ for every $X\subseteq A$ (trivially also for $X=\emptyset$).

**Lemma.** For every finite $D\subseteq G$: $|A+B+D|\le K|B+D|$.

*Proof by induction on $|D|$.* For $|D|=1$, $D=\{x\}$, both sides are translates: $|A+B+x|=|A+B|=K|B|=K|B+x|$.

Assume the claim for $D$ and let $x\notin D$, $D'=D\cup\{x\}$. Let
$$B_1=\{b\in B:\ b+x\in B+D\}.$$
- $B+D'=(B+D)\cup\big((B\setminus B_1)+x\big)$, and the union is disjoint by the definition of $B_1$. Hence $|B+D'|=|B+D|+|B|-|B_1|$.
- $A+B+D'=(A+B+D)\cup(A+B+x)$. If $a\in A$, $b\in B_1$, then $b+x\in B+D$, so $a+b+x\in A+B+D$; i.e. $A+B_1+x\subseteq A+B+D$. Therefore the elements of $A+B+x$ not already in $A+B+D$ lie in $(A+B+x)\setminus(A+B_1+x)$, which has $|A+B|-|A+B_1|$ elements (as $A+B_1\subseteq A+B$). So
$$|A+B+D'|\le|A+B+D|+|A+B|-|A+B_1|.$$

Using the induction hypothesis, $|A+B|=K|B|$ and $|A+B_1|\ge K|B_1|$:
$$|A+B+D'|\le K|B+D|+K|B|-K|B_1|=K|B+D'|. \qquad\square$$

**Iterating.** We show $|kA+B|\le K^k|B|$ for all $k\ge1$. For $k=1$ this is the definition of $K$. If it holds for $k$, the Lemma with $D=kA$ gives
$$|(k+1)A+B|=|A+B+kA|\le K|B+kA|\le K\cdot K^k|B|.$$

**Conclusion.** Pick $b\in B$. Then $kA+b\subseteq kA+B$, so
$$|kA|=|kA+b|\le|kA+B|\le K^k|B|\le c^k|A|,$$
since $K\le c$ and $|B|\le|A|$. ∎
